--- title: "The items behind the scales" subtitle: "Survey items, scales, reliability and missing answers" bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-missing.bib] --- In the Europeanisation and the economy case study, every outcome on the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) is built from one survey question, and the six scales that the full menu offers as its frame set are six ways of adding up the answers to it, of which the curve of the claim keeps the three positive ones. The menu treats the choice among them as a decision about what the claim is about, and the choice of scoring rule, a share of a respondent's own mentions or a count of the items in the set, as a second decision of the same kind. It does not, however, show the instrument itself. This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) takes the thirteen answer options apart: how often each is named, how the answers to them hang together, how many dimensions they hold, whether those dimensions are the four that the original author (OA) of the case study built and the course inherits, how far a scale of two items can be trusted as a measure, and what becomes of the respondents who name none of the thirteen. The subject is measurement rather than modelling. Nothing here changes which scales the course uses, for reasons that are given in section 8, but the module should leave you knowing more about the numbers before you choose one. The tables of sections 1 to 9 are read from files that were written before the page was built. The respondent-level records are GESIS-licensed and are not distributed with the course, so the analyses were run once, on the facilitator's machine, by `companion/_model-outputs/fit_measurement.R`, and only aggregate tables were committed: item prevalences, a correlation matrix, eigenvalues, loadings and fit indices. The correlation matrix is enough to repeat every exploratory step below without the microdata, and the [Try it](#try-it) at the end of the module does so. ## 1. The instrument {#sec-instrument} The question is the Eurobarometer item that asks "What does the European Union mean to you personally?", with a card of fourteen answers of which any number may be chosen, and it is the source of every framing scale in the case study. OA sets one of the fourteen aside, the Euro, and builds the four scales from the remaining thirteen [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623], grounding the grouping in an earlier categorical principal component analysis of a single wave which had found that "these answer categories build four distinct dimensions of EU framing across the 27 EU countries" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. The construction of each scale is stated in one sentence: "For each of the framing dimensions, the scale is composed of the sum of the mentioned items belonging to the specific framing dimension, divided by the total number of items mentioned by the respondent", so that the four scales "measure the relative frequency with which the respondent associates each frame to the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. That sentence is the share rule of the menu, and the count rule and the per-item rate are the two departures from it that the analysts of the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] and the course have taken. @tbl-items lists the thirteen answers under the scale to which each was assigned, with the share of all 416,698 respondents who named it. The course adds two composites to the four published scales, a positive one made of the cosmopolitan and utilitarian items together and a negative one made of the communitarian and libertarian items together, because the claim under test speaks of positive and negative dimensions in the plural and singles out none of them. ::: {#tbl-items .cell tbl-cap='The thirteen answer options, the scale each was assigned to in the original paper, and the share of respondents naming each. The \'Euro\' option is the fourteenth and is set aside throughout, following the original paper. Shares are over all respondents interviewed in the sixteen waves, those who named nothing included.'} ```{.r .cell-code} prev |> datawizard::data_modify(scale = factor(scale, scale_order), valence = dplyr::if_else(valence == "positive", "positive", "negative")) |> datawizard::data_arrange("scale") |> dplyr::transmute(Item = item, Scale = as.character(scale), Valence = valence, `Named by` = pct(share_mentioning)) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 4, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Item Scale Valence Named by
Peace cosmopolitan positive 28.5%
Democracy cosmopolitan positive 21.9%
Freedom to travel cosmopolitan positive 51.0%
Cultural diversity cosmopolitan positive 22.1%
Stronger say in the world cosmopolitan positive 23.1%
Economic prosperity utilitarian positive 18.7%
Social protection utilitarian positive 11.9%
Unemployment communitarian negative 16.6%
Loss of cultural identity communitarian negative 12.1%
More crime communitarian negative 17.5%
Not enough border control communitarian negative 16.6%
Bureaucracy libertarian negative 21.5%
Waste of money libertarian negative 21.6%
``` ::: ::: Freedom to travel is the one answer that about half of respondents give, and the rest are named by between roughly a tenth and three tenths, with social protection and the loss of cultural identity the rarest. Those prevalences matter for what follows, because a scale is only as informative as the answers it is made of, and a scale of two rarely named items has less to work with than a scale of five common ones. ## 2. The theory behind the grouping {#sec-theory} The four published scales are a theory, stated before any correlation was computed, and the paper sets it out in one sentence: the items "can be clustered into four distinct EU-framing dimensions endorsed by European citizens: two positive and two negative; two referring to a materialist and two related to a non-materialist understanding of the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 620]. Two axes cross. Valence separates the answers that praise the Union from the answers that blame it. Materialism separates the answers about money and welfare from the answers about peace, democracy, identity and borders. Each scale is one cell of the resulting two-by-two. The utilitarian scale is "the positive materialist dimension", the libertarian scale "the negative materialist dimension", the cosmopolitan scale "the positive non-materialist dimension" and the communitarian scale "the negative non-materialist dimension" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 620]. The paper relies on that design again in its hypotheses, which is why it is worth examining here. The first hypothesis has two sentences, and only the first of them appears on the claim card of the robustness study: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621]. The second sentence compares cells of the two-by-two with one another, and the comparison presupposes that the two materialist scales and the two non-materialist scales are what the theory says they are. The second hypothesis, about the education gap, makes the same presupposition when it predicts that poor economic performance narrows the gap more on the materialist dimensions. The sections that follow put to the data the question that the theory answered in advance: how do the thirteen answers hang together, and how many dimensions do they hold? The valence axis will come through clearly. The materialist axis will come through on one side of the valence line and not on the other, and section 8 says what that leaves of the two sentences above. Neither kind of grouping is wrong in itself. A scale defined by theory can be compared with published work and with other analysts, which is what a replication needs, while a scale defined by the data fits the data from which it was cut. The two groupings can disagree, and here they partly do, so the grouping on which a claim is tested is a decision that the analyst makes, whether or not the decision is stated. ## 3. The correlations among the items {#sec-correlations} Each answer is a yes or a no. The ordinary correlation cannot reach one between two yes-or-no variables that are named by different shares of respondents, so that an item named by a quarter of respondents and an item named by half can never correlate at more than about 0.58 however closely they go together. The usual remedy in measurement work is the tetrachoric correlation, which treats each binary answer as the visible part of an underlying continuous propensity to give it and estimates the correlation between the two propensities. It is the correlation that factor analysis of binary items is built on, and @fig-tet shows all seventy-eight of them, arranged with the two positive scales first and the two negative ones after. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tet_plot <- tet |> datawizard::data_modify(item = factor(item, item_order), with = factor(with, rev(item_order))) ggplot2::ggplot(tet_plot, ggplot2::aes(item, with, fill = tetrachoric)) + ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white") + ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = round(100 * tetrachoric)), size = 3, colour = dplyr::if_else(abs(tet_plot$tetrachoric) > 0.45, "white", "#1a1a1a")) + ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#96131b", mid = "white", high = "#0e3b6a", limits = c(-0.6, 0.6), name = "tetrachoric r") + ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 13 - 7 + 0.5, colour = "#3c4a56") + ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 7.5, colour = "#3c4a56") + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(), legend.position = "right") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Tetrachoric correlations among the thirteen items, times one hundred, over all respondents. Items are ordered by the scale they were assigned to: cosmopolitan and utilitarian above the line, communitarian and libertarian below it.](measurement_files/figure-html/fig-tet-1.png){#fig-tet width=787.2} ::: ::: The items divide first by valence. The seven positive items correlate positively with one another, at between roughly 0.12 and 0.44, the six negative items likewise at between 0.23 and 0.54, and the correlations across the line are close to zero or mildly negative, the strongest of them being the −0.30 between economic prosperity and waste of money. The original paper reports the same shape at the level of the four scales, with "the two positive EU framing and … the two negative EU-framing dimensions" associated at 0.27 and 0.26 and the associations across the valence line "low" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 625]. The item-level matrix also shows where the structure within each valence lies. On the negative side the two libertarian items, bureaucracy and waste of money, correlate at 0.50 with each other and more weakly with the communitarian four, while more crime and border control correlate at 0.54. On the positive side the strongest pairs, social protection with economic prosperity at 0.44, peace with democracy at 0.43 and freedom to travel with cultural diversity at 0.42, each lie within a published scale, but democracy correlates with social protection at 0.39 and with freedom to travel at only 0.22, so that the utilitarian pair are more closely related to peace and democracy than are freedom to travel and cultural diversity, the two mobility items of the cosmopolitan scale to which peace and democracy also belong. That is the first sign of what the factor analysis below makes explicit. The unemployment item, which the original paper counts among the communitarian meanings of the EU, bears on a decision elsewhere on the menu. It correlates at −0.19 with economic prosperity and at −0.18 with freedom to travel, and it is the item that a robustness check in the paper removes from the communitarian scale because "it could be theoretically argued that unemployment does not constitute a component of a communitarian understanding of the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 633, fn. 5]. The menu offers that removal as its item-set decision. ## 4. Dimensions {#sec-dimensions} A correlation matrix of thirteen items has thirteen eigenvalues, and their sizes indicate how much of the shared variation among the items a given number of underlying dimensions would account for. @fig-eigen plots them. The first two stand well clear of the rest, at 3.39 and 2.40, a third is at 1.13, and everything after it falls below one, which is the conventional line for a dimension worth keeping. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(eig, ggplot2::aes(factor, eigenvalue)) + ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = parallel_mean), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5b6b78") + ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a") + ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2.2) + ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#b7c2cc") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:13) + ggplot2::labs(x = "dimension", y = "eigenvalue") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Eigenvalues of the tetrachoric matrix (points), with the mean eigenvalue of random data of the same size (dashed) from a parallel analysis. With over four hundred thousand respondents the random benchmark is almost exactly one, so the parallel analysis is a formality here, and what matters is the size of the gaps between the eigenvalues.](measurement_files/figure-html/fig-eigen-1.png){#fig-eigen width=624} ::: ::: Read as a count of dimensions, the figure suggests two with a possible third, and the count rests on the items alone, without any assumption about which answers belong together. Two dimensions would be the valence split that the correlation matrix has already shown, and the next section asks whether a third and a fourth are the published split within each valence. The parallel analysis that is usually consulted at this point, which compares each eigenvalue with what random data of the same dimensions would produce, suggests five, but with 416,698 respondents the random benchmark is almost exactly one for every dimension, so that criterion reduces to counting eigenvalues above one and has little to add at this sample size. ## 5. Exploratory solutions {#sec-efa} Exploratory factor analysis asks which underlying dimensions, unconstrained by any prior assignment, best reproduce the correlations among the items, and reports for each item how strongly it belongs to each dimension. The solutions below were extracted by minimum-residual factoring from the tetrachoric matrix and rotated obliquely, which allows the dimensions to correlate with one another as substantive dimensions of an attitude generally do. @tbl-efa4 gives the four-factor solution, with the assignment made in the original paper beside each item, and loadings below 0.30 blanked so that the structure can be read at a glance; the two-factor solution follows in prose. ::: {#tbl-efa4 .cell tbl-cap='The four-factor exploratory solution (minimum residual, oblimin rotation), accounting for 43.9% of the variance in the items. Loadings under 0.30 are blank. Communality is the share of the variance of an item that the four factors reproduce together. Factor correlations: 1 with 4, 0.41; 2 with 3, 0.58; every positive factor with every negative one between −0.16 and −0.02.'} ```{.r .cell-code} show <- function(x) dplyr::if_else(abs(x) < 0.30, "", num(x)) l4 |> datawizard::data_modify(item = factor(item, item_order)) |> datawizard::data_arrange("item") |> dplyr::transmute(Item = as.character(item), `Published scale` = scale, `Factor 1` = show(F1), `Factor 2` = show(F2), `Factor 3` = show(F3), `Factor 4` = show(F4), Communality = num(communality)) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:7, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Item Published scale Factor 1 Factor 2 Factor 3 Factor 4 Communality
Peace cosmopolitan 0.51 0.32
Democracy cosmopolitan 0.60 0.42
Freedom to travel cosmopolitan 0.71 0.49
Cultural diversity cosmopolitan 0.48 0.41
Stronger say in the world cosmopolitan 0.35 0.30 0.30
Economic prosperity utilitarian 0.54 0.37
Social protection utilitarian 0.72 0.47
Unemployment communitarian 0.52 0.40
Loss of cultural identity communitarian 0.40 0.28
More crime communitarian 0.83 0.67
Not enough border control communitarian 0.63 0.43
Bureaucracy libertarian 0.75 0.53
Waste of money libertarian 0.62 0.62
``` ::: ::: Two of the four factors reproduce the two negative scales of the original paper, item for item. The communitarian four, unemployment, loss of cultural identity, more crime and border control, load on one factor and on nothing else, with more crime the strongest at 0.83; bureaucracy and waste of money load on a factor of their own at 0.75 and 0.62. The two are distinct and related, correlating at 0.58, which is the pattern one would want from two dimensions of a single negative stance towards the EU. The positive side does not reproduce the published split. Peace, democracy, economic prosperity and social protection form one factor, cutting across the line between cosmopolitan and utilitarian framing, and it is the two utilitarian items that load highest on it; freedom to travel and cultural diversity form another, with stronger say in the world divided between the two at 0.35 and 0.30. Read substantively, the data split the positive meanings of the EU not into a civic and an economic set but into a set of benefits that the EU delivers, peace and democracy alongside prosperity and protection, and a set of things that the EU lets one do and be, travel and diversity, with a stronger say in the world belonging a little to each. The two positive factors correlate at 0.41, which is lower than the correlation between the two negative ones. The two-factor solution is simpler still, and it is the solution to which the eigenvalues point first. Every positive item loads on one factor, at between 0.44 and 0.62, every negative item on the other, at between 0.51 and 0.75, no item loads above 0.30 on the wrong side, and the two factors correlate at −0.19. That is a clean valence structure, and it is the structure behind the two composites that the course adds: a positive scale of seven items and a negative scale of six are what the instrument most plainly measures, and each of the finer scales is a subset of one of them. ## 6. A confirmatory comparison {#sec-cfa} An exploratory solution is chosen by the data, so it is bound to fit the data it was chosen from. A confirmatory model states an assignment of items to dimensions in advance and asks how far the correlations it implies depart from the correlations found. @tbl-cfa compares three such models, fitted to the binary items by diagonally weighted least squares, the estimator built for this kind of data: the published four-scale model, the four-factor model read off @tbl-efa4 with stronger say in the world allowed to belong to both positive factors, and the two-factor valence model. The indices are the usual ones. The comparative fit index and the Tucker–Lewis index read upward towards one, and the root mean square error of approximation and the standardised root mean square residual read downward towards zero. By the customary thresholds a comparative fit index above 0.95 and a root mean square error below 0.05 count as good, and the chi-square is reported for completeness only, because with 416,698 respondents it rejects every model that is not exactly true. ::: {#tbl-cfa .cell tbl-cap='Three confirmatory models of the thirteen items, fitted on all respondents with the diagonally weighted least squares estimator and robust corrections. The data-driven model is the four-factor exploratory structure refitted as a confirmatory one, and is expected to fit better than the published model on the data it was read from.'} ```{.r .cell-code} cfa |> datawizard::data_modify(model = c(published = "Published four scales", data_driven = "Data-driven four factors", valence = "Two valence factors")[model]) |> dplyr::transmute(Model = model, `Chi-square (df)` = sprintf("%s (%d)", format(round(chisq), big.mark = ","), as.integer(df)), CFI = num(cfi, 3), TLI = num(tli, 3), RMSEA = num(rmsea, 3), SRMR = num(srmr, 3)) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:6, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Model Chi-square (df) CFI TLI RMSEA SRMR
Published four scales 42,153 (59) 0.910 0.882 0.041 0.060
Data-driven four factors 36,257 (58) 0.923 0.896 0.039 0.056
Two valence factors 57,825 (64) 0.877 0.850 0.047 0.071
``` ::: ::: The three models order as the exploratory analysis leads one to expect, and none of them reaches the conventional threshold of 0.95 on the comparative fit index. The data-driven model does best on every index, with a comparative fit index of 0.923 against 0.910 for the published scales and 0.877 for the valence model, and the root mean square error is below 0.05 for all three, at 0.039, 0.041 and 0.047. The published scales are a defensible reading of the items, though not a privileged one. A structure read off the data fits better, as it is bound to, and the difference between the two is confined to the positive side, where economic prosperity and social protection load with peace and democracy instead of forming a scale of their own. At the same time, the finer structure improves on the valence split by a margin that is real but modest, so a reader who prefers the two composites for their reliability, which the next section quantifies, or for their fit to the wording of the claim, gives up less than the four-scale vocabulary suggests. ## 7. Reliability {#sec-reliability} How far a short scale, such as one of two answers, can be trusted as a measure of a single disposition is a standard question in measurement, answered by a reliability coefficient. @tbl-rel gives, for the four published scales and the two composites, the number of items, their mean tetrachoric correlation, and the ordinal alpha that follows from the two, which is Cronbach's alpha computed on the tetrachoric rather than the ordinary correlations and read on the same scale, one being perfect consistency among the items. ::: {#tbl-rel .cell tbl-cap='Reliability of the six scales on the menu, from the tetrachoric correlations among their items. Ordinal alpha is Cronbach\'s alpha computed on the tetrachoric matrix. Mean prevalence is the average share of respondents naming an item of the scale.'} ```{.r .cell-code} rel |> datawizard::data_modify(scale = factor(scale, c(scale_order, "positive", "negative"))) |> datawizard::data_arrange("scale") |> dplyr::transmute(Scale = as.character(scale), Items = items, `Mean tetrachoric r` = num(mean_tetrachoric), `Ordinal alpha` = num(ordinal_alpha), `Mean prevalence` = pct(mean_prevalence)) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Scale Items Mean tetrachoric r Ordinal alpha Mean prevalence
cosmopolitan 5 0.31 0.69 29.3%
utilitarian 2 0.44 0.61 15.3%
communitarian 4 0.40 0.73 15.7%
libertarian 2 0.50 0.67 21.6%
positive 7 0.30 0.75 25.3%
negative 6 0.37 0.78 17.7%
``` ::: ::: The two composites are the most reliable constructs on the menu, at 0.75 and 0.78, because reliability grows with the number of items as well as with their agreement, and the two two-item scales are the least, the utilitarian at 0.61 and the libertarian at 0.67, although the two libertarian items agree with each other more closely than the items of either positive scale do. In the country-year panel on which the course fits its models, a low reliability means that the cell mean of a two-item scale is noisier for the same number of respondents, so that an association with unemployment is harder to detect on the utilitarian scale than on the cosmopolitan one, for a reason unrelated to whether the association exists. Reliability is a property of the construct, which is why the menu does not offer it as a choice. It still bears on the choice of outcome, and it is one of the reasons for the care with which the outcome axis is read on the results page. ## 8. Consequences for the menu {#sec-menu} When the results are set against the theory of section 2, the valence axis is recovered in full, and the first division among the items is between praise and blame. The materialist axis is recovered on the negative side, where the communitarian and libertarian items come apart exactly as the paper assigns them, and not on the positive side, where the items divide into the benefits that the Union delivers (peace, democracy, prosperity, social protection) and the mobility and diversity it permits (freedom to travel, cultural diversity), a line that cuts across the utilitarian and cosmopolitan scales. The second sentence of the first hypothesis, "the effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions", is thereby left as a comparison in which one of the two materialist scales is supported by the data and the other is a theoretical grouping that the data do not reproduce. The claim card that the analysts of the robustness study received contained the first sentence only, so none of the five reanalyses tested the comparison. This course does not test it either: the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-questions) sets out the sentence of the paper from which the claim was taken, and the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd) and the exercise page of each format explain why choosing which sentence to replicate is itself the first specification decision. The full menu keeps the four published scales and the two composites as its frame set, in the knowledge of what the analyses on this page show about each of them. The published scales are the vocabulary of the claim under test and of the five reanalyses, and comparability with both is worth more to a replication exercise than a structure that fits a little better on the data it was read from. The two negative scales are, in any case, recovered by the data item for item. The composites were added by the course, and they have the strongest support in the items: the valence split is the first thing the eigenvalues show, the two-factor solution is clean, and the composites are the most reliable scales on the menu. The curve of the claim keeps three of the six, the cosmopolitan and utilitarian scales and the positive composite, because the claim names the positive dimensions, and section 9 explains where the three negative scales went. The page argues against treating the assignment of items to scales as a further fork of the multiverse. Which items make up 'cosmopolitan framing' is a question about the validity of a measure of a named construct, and the evidence above is the right kind of evidence for it. Which construct the claim is about is a separate matter, so a menu that offered alternative groupings as options would be asking participants to settle by choice a question that the item analyses have already addressed. The scoring rule is a different kind of decision, one about the question itself, since whether a respondent's answers enter as a share of their own mentions or as a count of the items in the set changes what 'more cosmopolitan framing' means, and no analysis of the items can settle it. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimand) presents the three rules as a decision about the question, and section 9 sets out why the count and the rate left the curve. ## 9. The outcome on the curve {#sec-curve-outcome} When the course asked of every option on its menu whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim, read as a claim about change within countries over time, three of the decisions made on this page came out in a way that the full menu does not show. The [decision map](../menu.qmd#map) lays out every option of every decision, on the curve and off it, and the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) gives the reasoning for each; this section takes the three that concern the construction of the outcome. The numbers come from the curve of the claim (`data/spec_curve.csv`), the curve of the negative scales (`data/spec_curve_negative.csv`) and the comparison of every option of the full menu with its twins on the curve (`data/menu_deviations.csv`), all fitted on country-year aggregates and classed, like every point of the curve, by CR2 errors clustered by country with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. ### The negative scales {#sec-negative} The claim under test names the positive dimensions of framing, and the hypothesis from which it was taken has a second half, that poor economic performance increases the negative ones [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621]. The communitarian and libertarian scales and the negative composite answer that second half on a curve of their own, made of the same 864 specifications and drawn by the [Specification curve page](../curve.qmd#negative-scales) beside the curve of the claim: 68.1% of its specifications lie in the direction of the hypothesis with CR2 p < 0.05, against 77.2% on the curve of the claim. The two curves are not independent confirmations, for the reasons given under [Frame set](../menu.qmd#frame-set) in the specification menu and in the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-europeanisation). Reversed so that it points the way of the claim, the negative composite is the positive composite plus the rate of saying nothing, and once the mean of each country is removed the two correlate at 0.95 across the 270 country-years. The communitarian scale contains the item 'unemployment', which ties the outcome to the predictor by content, and at the reproduced specification its claim-aligned partial correlation is −0.495 with all thirteen items and −0.290 without that one. The libertarian scale moves little with the economy, 44.4% of its specifications lying in the direction of the hypothesis with CR2 p < 0.05 against 71.2% of the communitarian ones. ### Count and rate {#sec-count} The paper scores each scale as a share of the mentions of the respondent, and the curve keeps that rule because the claim concerns how citizens frame the EU, a matter of composition; the section [Scoring rule](../menu.qmd#scoring-rule) of the specification menu gives the reasoning. A count of the items of the scale that a respondent mentions measures how much the respondent says about the EU in that register, and across the 270 country-years it mostly tracks how much respondents say about the EU at all: the cosmopolitan count correlates at 0.85 with the mean number of items that respondents in the cell mention, the cosmopolitan share at −0.07, and the two versions of the same scale with each other at only 0.44. The count is the construct used by the reanalysts KEVF1 and 018OL, and the per-item rate, the count divided by the number of items in the scale, answers the same question about volume, since dividing by a constant leaves the test and the partial correlation of a linear model unchanged. Swapped into the 864 specifications of the curve, the count leaves 99.8% of them below zero but only 50.9% below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against 77.2% on the curve itself, and it changes the class of 33.7% of the pairs. At the reproduced specification the claim-aligned partial correlation falls from −0.242 with the share to −0.061 with the count, with a CR2 p-value of 0.63. ### The item set {#sec-item-set} Both item sets stay on the curve, as the section [Item set](../menu.qmd#item-set) of the specification menu explains: the thirteen items are the published measure, and the set without 'unemployment' removes a content overlap between outcome and predictor, since the item enters the denominator of every share and a rise in its mentions lowers every other share mechanically. The original paper removes the item from the communitarian scale in a robustness check [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 633, fn. 5], and the course set drops it from every denominator. On the curve of the claim 82.6% of the specifications with all thirteen items lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against 71.8% of those without the item; the decision carries 3.1% of the variance of the curve, moving it alone changes the class of 10.9% of the pairs of specifications that differ in nothing else, and at the reproduced specification the claim-aligned partial correlation moves from −0.242 to −0.194. The difference between the two sets is the part of the result that the overlap carries, and the curve keeps both so that the size of that part stays visible. ## 10. Respondents who mention nothing {#sec-noop} The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) has a decision called **respondents who mention nothing** with five options, and this section and the next explain why it is there. Of the 416,698 respondents, 26,325 (6.3%) answered the question of section 1 by mentioning none of the thirteen items, so that on every framing scale their score is zero divided by zero. The original paper and its five reanalyses resolved that in two different ways, mostly without saying so, and the people concerned are not a random slice of the sample. The curve of the claim keeps both of the two common rules, scoring the silent respondents zero and leaving them out, and the other three options are taught here beside the two rules. The survey records two further codes for a respondent who ticks nothing, "other (spontaneous)" and "don't know", and the 26,325 split three ways: 13,736 said they did not know, 3,642 gave an answer that was not on the list, and 8,947 have no tick of any kind. These are three different kinds of respondent. Someone who says the EU means something that the list did not anticipate has an opinion. Someone who says they do not know may have none, or may have one they would rather not state. A blank row may be a refusal, an omission by the interviewer or a coding gap, and the file does not say which. The Stata code written by OA divides the number of mentions in each framing cluster by the total number of mentions and has no rule for a zero total. Stata returns a missing value for 0/0, and the mixed model drops a missing outcome, so those respondents left the analysis of OA without a line of code saying so. The level-1 N of 390,373 that OA reported, the number of respondents in the model, is exactly the number who mentioned at least one item. The code of the reanalyst KQXUE drops them in the same way. The reanalysis that produced the t of −3.804 recorded in the robustness study coded the same respondents 0 on every scale, and the course panel inherits that convention, while KEVF1 and 018OL, who built a count and a mean of the cosmopolitan items rather than a share, score them 0 by construction. PRL47 built both versions and reported model B8, which uses the version without them. So the published coefficient and its best-known reanalysis differ in what they assume about 6.3% of the sample, and neither states the assumption. Whether that matters depends on who the silent respondents are, and on which comparison the analysis makes. They are older, more often women, and across the 270 cells the no-opinion rate correlates at 0.24 with the unemployment rate and at −0.25 with the cosmopolitan scale. The rate also differs sharply between countries: it runs at 16.0% in ES and 14.9% in GB against 1.9% in CY. Those correlations are dominated by stable differences between countries, which the fixed-effects designs of the curve remove. Within countries, net of the movement common to all of them in a year, the rate falls slightly as unemployment rises (−0.0011 per point of unemployment, t = −2.8 with conventional errors and −1.25 with errors clustered by country), so that scoring the silent as zero pulls the slopes of the curve a little towards zero rather than in the direction of the claim. @tbl-noop-countries lists the four highest and the four lowest rates, each averaged over the years of its country. ::: {#tbl-noop-countries .cell tbl-cap='The four highest and four lowest no-opinion rates, each averaged over the years of its country. The rules change the cell means before any model is fitted, and the average cosmopolitan cell mean is 0.507 under zero and 0.540 under drop. The rules also change the question. Under zero the estimand is the average framing among everyone interviewed, with silence counted as no framing, and the cell mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, so that the rate of saying nothing enters every scale. Under drop it is the average framing among people who have a framing at all, which suits the share as a measure, since a respondent with no mentions has no share, at the cost of conditioning on answering. Those are different populations, so by the test that is applied in the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#what-each-decision-commits-you-to) the no-opinion rule is an estimand decision. It is classed with measurement on the menu because that is where the decision is made in practice, at the moment the outcome column is built, and a participant who meets it there should know that it also changes the estimand. Both rules stay on the curve, zero because the reproduction task rests on it and drop because it matches the construct and the code of the original study. Split stays off it, since its construct is no clearer than that of either rule and its results lie close to theirs. Multiple imputation {#sec-imputation} Imputation replaces a rule with a model. Instead of deciding what the silent would have said, it estimates a distribution for each missing score from the observed characteristics of the respondent and draws from it, several times over, so that the uncertainty of the guess is included in the final standard error. @Dong2013Principled describe the three steps: fill the gaps m times to produce m complete datasets, analyse each with the model you would have run anyway, and combine the m results with the rules that @Rubin1987Imputation gave, under which the pooled estimate is the mean of the m estimates and its variance is the mean within-imputation variance plus the between-imputation variance inflated by a factor of 1 + 1/m. The between-imputation part expresses the uncertainty about the imputed values, and a single imputation, which sets it to zero, understates every standard error computed from it. How many imputations are enough depends on how much information is missing; @Graham2007Many show that the once-standard three to five are too few when the fraction of missing information is not small, and the course uses ten. The imputation model should include every variable in the analysis model and anything else that predicts either the missing values or their missingness [@CollinsEtAl2001ComparisonInclusiveRestrictive; @Schafer2002View], and it should not be *less* general than the analysis model, a condition that @Meng1994Imputation named 'congeniality', and one that is easy to violate here, since the imputation happens at respondent level and the analysis at cell level. Whether such a model can stand in for the missing answers depends on why the answers are missing. The vocabulary for this comes from @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData and is set out accessibly by @Dong2013Principled. Data are **missing completely at random** when the probability that a value is missing depends on nothing in the data at all, so the observed cases are a random sample of the complete ones; dropping the incomplete cases costs precision and nothing else. Data are **missing at random** when that probability depends on things that were observed but not, once those are accounted for, on the missing value itself. Data are **missing not at random** when the probability depends on the missing value even after the observed data are allowed for. The labels describe the mechanism that produced the gaps, not their size, and the practical consequence is asymmetric: the first two can be handled with methods that use only the observed data, while the third requires the analyst to say how the missing values differ from the observed ones, which the data cannot reveal. Mapped onto the case study, the silent respondents are plainly not missing completely at random, since their age, sex and location predict their silence. Missing at random given age, sex, education and the country-year cell is the working assumption that every imputation below rests on. It is not testable from the observed data alone, a point that @Dong2013Principled make against the habit of reading a t-test on observed covariates as a test of it. What can be done is to make it more plausible by conditioning on everything that predicts silence, and then to ask how far the conclusion moves if it is wrong. That last step is the sensitivity band at the end of this section. A "don't know" about what the EU means is a fair candidate for missing not at random, because the people least engaged with the EU are the people least likely to have a framing of it, and disengagement is not in the data. Two engines are run on the case study, because they come from different traditions and the course should show both. **mice** [@Buuren2011Mice] imputes one variable at a time conditional on the others, cycling until the imputations settle, and the version used here draws each missing share from respondents with similar predicted values (predictive mean matching), which keeps every imputed score inside the range that a bounded scale can take [@White2010Imputation]. **Amelia** [@HonakerEtAl2011AmeliaIIProgram; @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical] fits one multivariate normal model to all the variables at once by expectation maximisation (an iterative algorithm for fitting a model to incomplete data) with bootstrapping, the approach that was developed by Gary King and colleagues for time-series cross-section data of this shape [@HonakerKing2010WhatMissingValues]. Amelia imputes by drawing from that model, and the imputed values can fall outside the unit interval and are then clipped, as 24.1% of its draws were here. Both condition on age, sex, education and the country and year of interview. Each of the ten completed respondent files is aggregated to country-year means, and the models are fitted on each and pooled at the standard measurement settings, for 780 combinations of outcome, adjustment, estimator, sample and regression weight, among them designs and samples that the curve does not keep. Because the imputations exist only at those settings, they cannot be crossed with the rest of the menu, and they stay off the curve as a check on the two rules that it keeps. ::: {#tbl-mi .cell tbl-cap='The reproduced specification under multiple imputation, pooled over ten imputations by Rubin\'s rules, with conventional and with clustered errors. The fraction of missing information is the share of the uncertainty about the coefficient that is due to the silent respondents. The gap between the imputed rows and the zero row of @tbl-noop-spec is the part of the reproduced result that the zero convention takes away. ### "Don't know" as an answer {#sec-dont-know} Survey methodologists have argued for fifty years about whether a "don't know" is missing data or a response. @Francis1975Know reviewed the early evidence; @Krosnick2001Impact showed experimentally that offering an explicit no-opinion option does not, in general, improve the quality of the answers that remain, because many who take it could have answered; and @Luskin2011Know found the reverse for factual knowledge, where "don't know" mostly does mean not knowing. @Kuha2018Effect distinguish three ways of asking (encouraging a "don't know", accepting one neutrally, and probing it with a follow-up) and show on European Social Survey data that probing halves the rate but changes the measurement properties of the answers it extracts, so that the survey has traded an error of omission for an error of commission. The ESS itself does not probe. Who says "don't know" is not random either: @Laurison2015WillingnessStateOpinion finds the willingness to state an opinion patterned by class and education, which makes non-response on attitude items a form of inequality in whose views reach the data. That literature has two implications for this case study. It supports treating a "don't know" about the EU as non-response rather than as zero framing, which is what the drop rule, the split rule and the imputations do. It also warns that a group defined by not answering cannot be assumed to resemble the group that did, so the missing-at-random assumption behind imputation is where a critic would press. The "other" code in the battery is more reassuring, since 3,642 people volunteered a meaning that the list did not offer, and each of those answers is an opinion. ### Sensitivity to the assumption {#sec-sensitivity} Nothing in the observed data can distinguish missing at random from missing not at random; @Molenberghs2008Missingness prove that for any model of the latter there is a model of the former that fits the observed data equally well. The response is to show how far the conclusion depends on the assumption, and the device used here is a sensitivity band. Suppose every silent respondent would have scored what the answering respondents in their cell scored, plus some amount δ that is the same for all of them. Then each cell mean is the answered mean plus δ times the share of the cell that was silent, and the reproduced specification can be refitted for any δ. Two values are already familiar. δ = 0 is the drop rule, and the zero rule sets δ to minus the answered mean of each cell, which averages about −0.53, so that a common δ of that size approximates it. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The partial correlation of cosmopolitan framing with unemployment, two-way fixed effects, when every silent respondent is assigned the answered mean of their cell plus δ. Zero on the horizontal axis is the drop rule; the dashed line marks the average δ of the zero rule, and the burgundy point the zero rule itself, which applies a different δ to each cell. Sources: `data/teney_panel_measurement.csv`, `data/teney_panel_weights.csv` and `data/spec_curve.csv`.](measurement_files/figure-html/fig-delta-1.png){#fig-delta width=672} ::: ::: The band runs in one direction. The further the silent respondents are assumed to fall short of those who answered, the weaker the association, from r = −0.332 at δ = 0.3 through −0.312 at δ = 0 to −0.260 at δ = −0.6, and the zero convention, which assumes that everyone who stayed silent would have scored the lowest value that the scale allows, is the most extreme assumption that the bounds of the scale permit, and among the assumptions that they permit it moves the result furthest towards zero. Every value on the band remains below zero, so the direction of the association does not depend on the assumption, while its strength does, and that is what should be reported alongside a result on these data. Reporting the missing-data treatment, the assumption it makes and the sensitivity of the result to that assumption is what @Lee2021Framework and @Sterne2009Imputation ask for in observational research, and the proportion of missing data is not, on its own, the thing to report [@MadleyDowd2019Proportion]. ## Try it {#try-it} The committed correlation matrix is all that the exploratory analyses need.
